subject: PS
title: Introduction to Modern Africa
info: Same as AFST 222, ANTH 222, and SOC 222. See AFST 222.

sections.sectionText: Modern Africa has sustained the most rapid and profound changes of any continent in the world. Indeed, the African continent saw its social systems, economic structures, political organizations, and religious and cultural practices profoundly transformed by centuries of European imperialism. Yet, Africa is still largely known in the United States through exotic images of the cultural “other,” decimated by civil wars, clan violence, famine, and HIV/AIDS. This course goes beyond these images and stereotypes to place Africa and its people within the shared history of an increasingly global world. The course will utilize an interdisciplinary framework to examine the great civilizations of pre-colonial African societies; the trans-Atlantic slave trade; the impact of colonialism, nationalism, Pan-Africanism, and nationalist and independence movements; social movements and democratization; gender and development; the role of the African Diaspora in Africa's development; and globalization. This course fulfills a general education requirement for Cultural Studies: Non-Western and American Minority Cultures, as well as Social Science.

sections.sectionText: Major restrictions will be lifted by noon on Monday, November 16, 2026. Climate change is less a collective-action problem than a fight over who pays and who profits. This seminar reads treaties, court rulings, and movement claims as political bargains, asking who wins, who loses, and whose voices shaped the law. It covers the UN climate regime, the politics of decarbonization and obstruction, energy transitions, petrostates, small island diplomacy, loss and damage, climate migration, and litigation from Pakistan to the ICJ. Students interview practitioners, expand Wikipedia’s coverage of Global South climate politics, and submit an op-ed or rulemaking comment to a real institution. No legal training required.

sections.sectionText: Major restrictions will be lifted by noon on Monday, November 16, 2026. The Information Revolution is changing the world in all sorts of ways. "Politics of the internet" explores how the internet has affected politics—including politicians' public communications, terrorist recruitment, foreign influence operations, campaigning, the structure and behavior of political media, and more—as well as political questions of the internet itself, such as social media content moderation and free speech. Students will be expected to attend and participate in discussions, write multiple papers, and present material to the class. Not available to students who have taken an advanced-level version of this class in SP22, SP23, SP25 or SP26. Not available to students who have taken this course as PS 199 in SP24.

sections.sectionText: Major restrictions will be lifted by noon on Monday, November 16, 2026. Title: Frantz Fanon’s Political Thought. Frantz Fanon is best known as a theorist of violence, colonialism, and revolution. This course will focus on his lesser-known writings on freedom, alienation, and psychiatric practice, which illuminate how social and political conditions shape our sense of self and our ways of being in the world. By exploring Fanon’s clinical and political writings, we will examine liberation as a process not only of political decolonization but also of subjective transformation and new forms of life.

sections.sectionText: This course examines the evolution of neofascist ideologies, movements, and regimes from 1945 to the present. We will analyze the ideological foundations of neofascism, the role of clandestine networks, and the impact of far-right extremism on contemporary politics. We will also discuss legal, philosophical, and historical debates over neofascist movements. This course involves analysis of primary sources from figures like Julius Evola, Aleksandr Dugin, Francis Parker Yockey, and Savitri Devi, as well as recent scholarship on the topic. (Meets with ITAL 390)

sections.sectionText: Language & Minorities in Europe. Credit: 3 or 4 hours. Survey of regional and immigrant minority language use, policies, and planning across Europe.
